Certain chambers are lined with generations of ancestors, though no names remain attached to individual shapes.
It cultivates impossible species—plants that photosynthesize in near-darkness, roots that crack stone with patient pressure, flowers that bloom once per century in colors that have no names.
They are called the Hollow Choir, though they have no name for themselves.
They have no name for themselves that a stranger could say.
Call them *tæmorosapients*, though they answer to no name shouted above a whisper.
In the processing facility, things dwell that have no name.
Beneath it all, threading through porous conglomerate and hairline fractures, runs a network that has no name but functions as a circulatory system.

And now this account of you exists, somewhere, in some form, and the terraces have been noticed, and the noticing is a kind of life too — fragile, brief, human-shaped, and as close to the unnamed builders as anything has come since they put down their tools and walked away into whatever lay beyond the horizon of their own creation.
It has no name it uses, and none that others remember.
The youngest ones, newly condensed, appear as ribbons of living glass, their bodies catching and refracting the chamber's strange light into spectra that include colors with no names.

They have no names that carry through the steam, but they are shaped roughly like tall, narrow steles of dry, pressed pith, ten to twelve feet in height, tapering toward the crown like old willow hampers.

They catch the light and they catch the air and they catch the moisture and they catch, in some way that involves the particular pattern of their spiral arrangement, something else — something that has no name in your physics because your physics never had reason to name it.
This is not a name they have for themselves, for they have no language, no collective noun.

They have no name for themselves that human tongues could pronounce; their identity exists in the chemical signals they exchange through the interconnected pools and in the vibrations they send through stone.
What lives here has no name for itself.
Not a name they would recognize—there is no recognition in them, only gradient and density and the endless bisecting of stone—but it is what the sound makes of them.
The people who live here have no name for themselves, for they have no concept of another kind of person.
They possess no name or concept of personal identity.
And then there is the thing that has no name, the thing that lives in the cirque the way a song lives in a throat before it is sung.
The people have no name for it that is separate from the seam at evening.
They have no name for themselves, for they have no language of words.

Call it the *Resident*, though it has no name for itself—only the continuous modulation of its own attention, which feels like the hum you hear when pressing your ear to a seashell that contains no sea.
They leave behind no stories of themselves, no names carved into stone, no chatter of memory that you could hear.

The chamber is keeping count with a tool it found, using a technology it did not invent, applying a competence it learned by watching, or by absorbing, or by some third method that has no name in your taxonomy of learning because it requires no brain, no nervous system, no center of cognition, only a distributed awareness that is dense enough and patient enough to observe a process and replicate it.
These entities have no names yet; they are called Shifts when traders need a word.
It has no name that Marta knows, and she's stopped looking for one.
The air itself is a living, breathing entity, thick with the scent of damp earth and the sweet fragrance of unnamed blossoms, carried on the gentle breeze that rustles through the leaves above.
It is sphagnum and liverwort and haircap and the black one that has no name and twenty other things grown into each other so completely that no root or rhizoid belongs to a single individual anymore.

Every weight that touches the moss is expected, because the moss expects everything, because expectation is what the moss *is* — a trillion tiny mouths open to the stone, waiting for whatever the stone offers, converting it, incorporating it, building it into the body of something that has no name and no boundary and no end.

Her tools materialize when she needs them: wrenches that exist only in the moment of turning, hammers that are hammers only while swinging, measuring devices that measure things she has no names for in units she understands perfectly.
It is not conscious co-cultivation; it is an emergent contract between nervous systems too small to house intention and microbial communities too diffuse to be named.
The hunters are called Twig-Jacks, though the name is too playful for them.
What lives in this place is not easily named.
They are called the Custodians, though no one named them and they do not name themselves.

There was a man on Station 7—his name is not recorded because he asked for it to be removed from the logs, which is a right written into every employment contract, and one that the company regrets extending but cannot legally revoke.

They have names for the big ones — the seven jacks that hold the waist of the bubble, where the compression is worst, have names the way boats have names, and are spoken of with the same wary affection.

**The carapaced things**—no one has named them properly because naming requires the assumption that classification matters—are the most visible inhabitants, though visibility is relative in a landscape where movement itself seems reluctant.
Sometimes, far under the peat, something changes its position, and the whole basin feels it: a low, unhurried adjustment beneath homes, gardens, birds, animals, memories, and names.
What lives here has no name for itself because names are for calling across distance, and there is no distance left that has not already been answered.
But each name would be too small.
They have no name for this place.
The prints fade by evening, consumed by oxidation and the morning rain, but they are the closest thing the place has to signing a name.
They would not demand a name.
” They name phases more confidently than places: Wet-Hanging, Salt-Tight, Deep-Heat, After-Breaking.
The world remembers them this way: not as names, but as extra grain, laid down along the load-lines to help the timber bear the terrifying, weightless height of its own impossible span.
Adults take a second name from their work, so that Drip Hookhand, Roar of the Kiln, and Whistle Lashwright are clear enough to any neighbor.
And if one must name its inhabitants more simply, then say this:
They have a word that means the memory of a solvent, and it is liturgical, used the way some peoples use the names of dead gods: carefully, and not in the house.
But now, in the hollow’s young and practical age, it is exactly the kind of life that fits: not green, not loud in itself, not charismatic, not separate from its habitat enough to be easily named.
But if you insist on bodies, on presences, on things that can be pointed to and named — then there are layers.
And then, there are the things that cannot be named.
Ask where someone ends and they may answer by naming a doorway, a tree, a troublesome patch of pavement.
Names are for things that can be called.
Sometimes, when the settlement inhales, they un-tuck and resume their gliding, leaving trails of glint that fade by morning like the memory of a name.
They have no names they speak aloud.
They can carry fragments of old shell, black reed seeds, tiny insects, and the larvae of animals not yet named.
The people once had names and errands and small metallic hopes (the dark copper fittings still gleam with ghost-polish where those hopes once rubbed).

These beings, which I might tentatively name the Veilscutters, embody the basin's weirdness, their bodies a blend of mammalian warmth and reptilian resilience, adapted to retain every drop of moisture in their thick, leathery hides.
Larvae, mites, pale segmented things with too many legs and not enough distinguishing features to name individually.
If you were to give them a name, you might call them the Anchored, or the Still.
Sunder does not have a name.
- A sky that is not a ceiling at all, but something they cannot name: an unbounded, stone-less above that refuses to press on them.
But the names have stuck, and when Dael comes in from the well-fields at dusk and sees the chipped one standing motionless at the pool's edge, they nod.
They’re curing racks, whether or not any mind in the system is consciously naming them.
It is still, in some way that you cannot name, *becoming*.
This is not because they lack language but because naming requires a fixed point — a moment when you can say *this is what I am* — and they have no such moment.
The ferns are the visible inhabitants, the ones you would name if someone asked you what grows in the Flue, but they are not the important ones.
